Hepatitis B Immunization Among Healthcare Students: A Narrative Review of Occupational Risk, Seroprotection, and Immunization Management

Authors: Lorenzo Ippoliti, Viola Giovinazzo, Luca Coppeta, Giuseppe Bizzarro, Cristiana Ferrari, Andrea Mazza, Agostino Paolino, Silvio Pallone, Matteo Pasanisi, Claudia Salvi
Original abstract (English)
Background/Objectives: Healthcare students face an occupational risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) exposure during clinical training, often many years after receiving their primary vaccination series in infancy or childhood. Progressive waning of anti-hepatitis B surface (anti-HBs) antibody titres, heterogeneous vaccination histories in international student cohorts, high rates of underreported needlestick injuries, and variable occupational health protocols across institutions raise important questions about the adequacy of pre-clinical immunization surveillance in this population. This review aimed to synthesize current evidence on hepatitis B immunization among healthcare students, focusing on occupational exposure risk, seroprotection and immunological memory, clinical management of low or absent anti-HB titres including post-exposure prophylaxis, and the specific challenges posed by multicultural academic settings. Methods: A narrative review was conducted through a systematic literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus, covering publications from January 2000 to December 2025, supplemented by key seminal references. After the removal of duplicates and stepwise screening, 49 references were selected for final inclusion. Results: Needlestick and sharps injuries occur at measurable rates during clinical training, with medical students accounting for approximately 30% of occupational exposure events in some series, and with underreporting rates estimated at 19–80% across studies. Pooled seroprotection prevalence at clinical training entry is approximately 73.8% (95% CI 69.1–78.0%), with substantially lower rates among students vaccinated in infancy—as low as 28% at 16–20 years post-vaccination in longitudinal data—compared with adolescence immunization. The majority of students with non-protective titres retain immunological memory, with 90.9% (95% CI 87.7–93.3%) demonstrating an anamnestic response after a single booster dose. Post-exposure prophylaxis pathways depend critically on pre-existing immunological status, reinforcing the operational value of pre-clinical serological screening. International student cohorts present additional complexity due to heterogeneous vaccination schedules, documentation gaps, and variable natural immunity profiles. Conclusions: Systematic pre-clinical serological screening (anti-HBs, HBsAg, and anti-HBc), combined with evidence-based stepwise immunization management and structured educational interventions, is essential to protect healthcare students from occupational HBV exposure. The primary operational goal of screening is the identification of the approximately 5% of true non-responders who require tailored occupational health management. These findings support a proactive, integrated approach to hepatitis B immunization surveillance in healthcare education, aligned with the WHO 2030 viral hepatitis-elimination targets.

Pooled seroprotection prevalence at clinical training entry is approximately 73.8% (95% CI 69.1–78.0%), with substantially lower rates among students vaccinated in infancy—as low as 28% at 16–20 years post-vaccination in longitudinal data—compared with adolescence immunization. The majority of students with non-protective titres retain immunological memory, with 90.9% (95% CI 87.7–93.3%) demonstrating an anamnestic response after a single booster dose. The primary operational goal of screening is the identification of the approximately 5% of true non-responders who require tailored occupational health management.

靶向 共价闭合环状DNA 进行降解:慢性乙型肝炎 感染背景下基于内源和外源的核定位 DNA 破坏方法

Targeting cccDNA for Degradation: Endogenous- and Exogenous-Based Methods of Nuclear-Localized DNA Destruction in the Context of Chronic Hepatitis B Infection
作者： Cassie Thompson, Vanessa Meier-Stephenson, Vanessa Meier‐Stephenson
摘要中文翻译促进细胞降解或实现目标有害DNA的治疗性破坏的能力被认为是各种病毒感染的治疗的主要目标。就 慢性乙型肝炎 而言,对受感染肝细胞核中发现的附加型病毒 基因组 进行靶向 DNA 降解是实现真正治愈的关键。然而,研究人员仍在研究没有过度大规模细胞毒性的靶向 DNA 降解机制。本综述总结了目前已知能够靶向核定位 DNA 的几种系统,包括可用于治疗的内源性 DNA 降解方法和外源性方法(如 CRISPR 或其他异生物质),重点关注它们在乙型肝炎 治疗 中的潜在应用。
查看综述五要素
范围与问题
该综述的重点是开发靶向和降解核定位 DNA 的方法,特别是在 慢性乙型肝炎 感染的情况下。核心问题是内源性或外源性系统是否可以在不引起过度细胞毒性的情况下实现对受感染肝细胞中附加型病毒 基因组 的治疗性破坏。
证据基础与方法
该综述是对当前能够靶向核定位 DNA 的系统的叙述性总结,包括内源性和外源性方法。它不报告特定数据库、检索日期或荟萃分析程序。所讨论的方法基于现有文献,并总结了它们在乙型肝炎中的潜在应用治疗。
共识与结论
该综述得出的结论是,靶向 DNA 降解是治疗各种病毒感染(尤其是 慢性乙型肝炎)的主要目标。它强调受感染肝细胞核中的游离病毒 基因组 是实现真正治愈的关键目标。然而,它也指出,没有过度细胞毒性的靶向 DNA 降解机制仍在研究中。
争议与缺口
该评论强调,虽然已经确定了几种用于靶向核定位 DNA 的系统,但对于最有效或毒性最小的方法尚未达成共识。此外,临床应用和长期安全性方面的证据有限,表明在理解如何将这些方法转化为治疗策略方面存在差距。
科研与实践启示
该综述表明,需要进一步研究来开发和完善靶向 DNA 降解方法,以最大限度地减少细胞毒性。这还意味着应该探索 CRISPR 和其他异生素等外源方法在乙型肝炎 治疗 中的潜力,重点关注其在临床环境中的有效性和安全性。

Targeting cccDNA for Degradation: Endogenous- and Exogenous-Based Methods of Nuclear-Localized DNA Destruction in the Context of Chronic Hepatitis B Infection

Authors: Cassie Thompson, Vanessa Meier-Stephenson, Vanessa Meier‐Stephenson
Original abstract (English)
The ability to facilitate cellular degradation or achieve therapeutic destruction of targeted noxious DNA is recognized as a major goal for the treatment of various viral infections. In the case of chronic hepatitis B, targeted DNA degradation of the episomal viral genome found in the nucleus of infected hepatocytes is key to achieving a true cure. However, mechanisms of targeted DNA degradation without excessive broadscale cytotoxicity are still under investigation by researchers. This review summarizes several current systems known to have the ability to target nuclear-localized DNA, including endogenous methods of DNA degradation that may be harnessed therapeutically and exogenous methods such as CRISPR or other xenobiotics, with a focus on their potential application in hepatitis B treatment.
View review five-element analysis
Scope and question
The review focuses on the development of methods to target and degrade nuclear-localized DNA, specifically in the context of chronic hepatitis B infection. The central question is whether endogenous or exogenous-based systems can achieve therapeutic destruction of the episomal viral genome in infected hepatocytes without causing excessive cytotoxicity.
Evidence base and method
The review is a narrative summary of current systems capable of targeting nuclear-localized DNA, including endogenous and exogenous methods. It does not report on specific databases, search dates, or meta-analysis procedures. The methods discussed are based on existing literature and are summarized for their potential application in hepatitis B treatment.
Consensus and conclusions
The review concludes that targeted DNA degradation is a major goal for treating various viral infections, particularly chronic hepatitis B. It emphasizes that the episomal viral genome in the nucleus of infected hepatocytes is a key target for achieving a true cure. However, it also notes that mechanisms for targeted DNA degradation without excessive cytotoxicity are still under investigation.
Controversies and gaps
The review highlights that while several systems have been identified for targeting nuclear-localized DNA, there is no consensus on the most effective or least toxic method. Additionally, the evidence is limited in terms of clinical application and long-term safety, indicating a gap in understanding how these methods can be translated into therapeutic strategies.
Research and practice implications
The review suggests that further research is needed to develop and refine methods for targeted DNA degradation that minimize cytotoxicity. It also implies that exogenous methods such as CRISPR and other xenobiotics should be explored for their potential in hepatitis B treatment, with a focus on their efficacy and safety in clinical settings.

慢性乙型肝炎 中核苷(酸)类似物戒断后结果的免疫相关性:直接证据、机制背景和候选生物标志物

Immune correlates of outcomes after nucleos(t)ide analogue withdrawal in chronic hepatitis B: direct evidence, mechanistic context, and candidate biomarkers
作者： Zihao Xu, Yifan Liu, Liangbin Cheng, Jun Xu
摘要中文翻译慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 中核苷类似物 (NA) 的停用会产生两种临床上不同的轨迹:少数患者实现乙型肝炎表面抗原 (HBsAg) 持续丧失或 治疗 病毒控制消失,而其他患者则出现肝炎发作,但没有病毒学益处。最近的纵向研究已开始定义这些结果的 宿主 免疫相关性。本小型综述将 NA 戒断 队列研究 的直接证据与其他 CHB 环境中获得的机械证据分开。直接人体数据表明,有益的结果与 HBsAg 特异性记忆 B 细胞活性的恢复、浆母细胞扩张、更强的 T 滤泡辅助协作以及保留 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV) 特异性 T 细胞功能有关。相比之下,整体 T 细胞上的高抑制性受体表达、持续的炎症趋化因子特征以及急性发作后更大的丙氨酸转氨酶变异性与非有益的发作相关。由 HBsAg 和 HBsAg 抗体形成的免疫复合物提供了额外的体液读数,可以反映 HBsAg 发作风险和 HBsAg 下降的质量。这些观察结果很有希望,但仍然是探索性的:队列研究 很小,耀斑定义不同,检测方法不标准化,并且大多数签名缺乏外部验证。因此,免疫标志物应被视为与病毒生物标志物、肝脏疾病严重程度和密切的停药后监测相结合的候选相关因素,而不是作为停止治疗的独立标准。
查看综述五要素
范围与问题
慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 中核苷类似物 (NA) 的停用会产生两种临床上不同的轨迹:少数患者实现乙型肝炎表面抗原 (HBsAg) 持续丧失或 治疗 病毒控制消失,而其他患者则出现肝炎发作,但没有病毒学益处。
证据基础与方法
最近的纵向研究已开始定义这些结果的 宿主 免疫相关性。本小型综述将 NA 戒断 队列研究 的直接证据与其他 CHB 环境中获得的机械证据分开。
共识与结论
直接人体数据表明,有益的结果与 HBsAg 特异性记忆 B 细胞活性的恢复、浆母细胞扩张、更强的 T 滤泡辅助协作以及保留 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV) 特异性 T 细胞功能有关。相比之下,整体 T 细胞上的高抑制性受体表达、持续的炎症趋化因子特征以及急性发作后更大的丙氨酸转氨酶变异性与非有益的发作相关。
争议与缺口
这些观察结果很有希望,但仍然是探索性的:队列研究 很小,耀斑定义不同,检测方法不标准化,并且大多数签名缺乏外部验证。
科研与实践启示
因此,免疫标志物应被视为与病毒生物标志物、肝脏疾病严重程度和密切的停药后监测相结合的候选相关因素,而不是作为停止治疗的独立标准。

Immune correlates of outcomes after nucleos(t)ide analogue withdrawal in chronic hepatitis B: direct evidence, mechanistic context, and candidate biomarkers

Authors: Zihao Xu, Yifan Liu, Liangbin Cheng, Jun Xu
Original abstract (English)
Nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) discontinuation in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) can produce two clinically divergent trajectories: a minority of patients achieve sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss or off-treatment viral control, whereas others develop hepatitis flares without virological benefit. Recent longitudinal studies have begun to define the host immune correlates of these outcomes. This Mini Review separates direct evidence from NA-withdrawal cohorts from mechanistic evidence obtained in other CHB settings. Direct human data suggest that beneficial outcomes are associated with recovery of HBsAg-specific memory B-cell activity, plasmablast expansion, stronger T follicular helper collaboration, and preserved hepatitis B virus (HBV)-specific T-cell function. In contrast, high inhibitory-receptor expression on global T cells, persistent inflammatory chemokine signatures, and greater post-flare alanine aminotransferase variability are associated with non-beneficial flares. immune complexes formed by HBsAg and antibodies to HBsAg provide an additional humoral readout that may reflect both flare risk and the quality of HBsAg decline. These observations are promising but remain exploratory: cohorts are small, flare definitions are heterogeneous, assays are not standardized, and most signatures lack external validation. Immune markers should therefore be viewed as candidate correlates to be integrated with viral biomarkers, liver-disease severity, and close post-withdrawal monitoring rather than as stand-alone criteria for stopping therapy.
View review five-element analysis
Scope and question
Nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) discontinuation in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) can produce two clinically divergent trajectories: a minority of patients achieve sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss or off-treatment viral control, whereas others develop hepatitis flares without virological benefit.
Evidence base and method
Recent longitudinal studies have begun to define the host immune correlates of these outcomes. This Mini Review separates direct evidence from NA-withdrawal cohorts from mechanistic evidence obtained in other CHB settings.
Consensus and conclusions
Direct human data suggest that beneficial outcomes are associated with recovery of HBsAg-specific memory B-cell activity, plasmablast expansion, stronger T follicular helper collaboration, and preserved hepatitis B virus (HBV)-specific T-cell function. In contrast, high inhibitory-receptor expression on global T cells, persistent inflammatory chemokine signatures, and greater post-flare alanine aminotransferase variability are associated with non-beneficial flares.
Controversies and gaps
These observations are promising but remain exploratory: cohorts are small, flare definitions are heterogeneous, assays are not standardized, and most signatures lack external validation.
Research and practice implications
Immune markers should therefore be viewed as candidate correlates to be integrated with viral biomarkers, liver-disease severity, and close post-withdrawal monitoring rather than as stand-alone criteria for stopping therapy.

SU-led collaboration tackles critical questions in hepatitis B treatment - Stellenbosch University
新闻简报一项新的国际研究合作项目 B-ZERO 获得了著名的 Wellcome Trust 发现奖,该奖项旨在调查为什么一些乙型肝炎患者尽管接受了 治疗 治疗,但仍无法抑制病毒。这项研究由来自南非、埃塞俄比亚、英国和挪威的研究人员领导,将探讨药物浓度、治疗 的获取以及非洲 HBV 毒株的差异等因素。该研究旨在改善 治疗 的结果,降低肝病和癌症风险,并加强努力消除非洲卫生系统中的病毒性肝炎。这项工作将重点关注乙型肝炎病毒流行的地区,包括埃塞俄比亚和南非,并将利用 HEPSANET 的数据,HEPSANET 是几个非洲国家病毒性肝炎患者的纵向登记系统。斯泰伦博斯大学副教授 Tongai Maponga 教授强调了了解非洲环境中的病毒性肝炎并将这些知识转化为改进的预防、诊断、治疗 和政策的重要性。该研究将解决有关 治疗 疗效的关键问题以及当地卫生系统管理 HBV 的挑战。

该研究重点关注乙型肝炎流行的埃塞俄比亚和南非地区。受影响人群包括乙型肝炎病毒感染患者,特别是非洲卫生系统中的患者。
事件
一项新的国际研究合作项目 B-ZERO 获得了 Wellcome Trust 发现奖,该项目旨在调查为什么一些乙型肝炎患者尽管接受了 治疗 治疗仍无法抑制病毒。这是根据报告中描述的研究计划确认的事件。

The study aims to improve treatment outcomes, reduce liver disease and cancer risk, and strengthen efforts to eliminate viral hepatitis in African health systems. 应对、状态与不确定性
该研究合作正在积极调查患者对替诺福韦(一种治疗乙型肝炎的一线 治疗)的反应。该研究涉及多个机构,并将利用现有纵向登记处 HEPSANET 的数据。这些发现预计将改善 治疗 的结果并解决有关 HBV 治疗 的未解决问题。
B routine priorityPublic-health news

SU-led collaboration tackles critical questions in hepatitis B treatment - Stellenbosch University

News Brief
A new international research collaboration, B-ZERO, has secured a prestigious Wellcome Trust Discovery Award to investigate why some hepatitis B patients fail to suppress the virus despite receiving treatment. The study, led by researchers from South Africa, Ethiopia, the UK, and Norway, will explore factors such as drug concentrations, access to treatment, and differences in African HBV strains. The research aims to improve treatment outcomes, reduce liver disease and cancer risk, and strengthen efforts to eliminate viral hepatitis in African health systems. The work will focus on regions where HBV is endemic, including Ethiopia and South Africa, and will draw on data from HEPSANET, a longitudinal registry of patients living with viral hepatitis in several African countries. Prof Tongai Maponga, associate professor at Stellenbosch University, emphasized the importance of understanding viral hepatitis in African settings and translating this knowledge into improved prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and policy. The study will address critical questions about treatment efficacy and the challenges of managing HBV in local health systems.

Sue Segar 25 August 2026 A new international research collaboration, B-ZERO, has secured a prestigious Wellcome Trust Discovery Award to investigate why some hepatitis B patients fail to suppress the virus despite receiving treatment. Researchers from South Africa, Ethiopia, the UK and Norway will study patient responses to tenofovir, exploring factors such as drug concentrations, access to treatment and differences in African HBV strains. The findings aim to improve hepatitis B treatment outcomes, reduce liver disease and cancer risk, and strengthen efforts to eliminate viral hepatitis in African health systems. Several serious questions remain unanswered regarding the treatment of patients with hepatitis B. For instance, why do some patients who carry the hepatitis B virus (HBV) suppress the virus while receiving treatment, whereas others do not? Could it be that they don’t have the correct concentrations of the drugs used to treat the virus in their blood to be able to suppress virus replication? Or is there something about the HBV strains in Africa that is different compared to other places? These are some of the questions that a team of researchers from South Africa, the United Kingdom, Ethiopia and Norway will tackle when they embark on a collaborative study aimed at understanding why some patients with HBV fail to achieve viral suppression despite receiving treatment. Funded through a Wellcome Trust Discovery Award, the research collaboration known as B-ZERO brings together colleagues from Stellenbosch University (SU), and the Universities of Cape Town, Addis Ababa, Bristol, and Oslo. Also involved are the Francis Crick Institute, a leading biomedical research centre in London, and the Vestfold Hospital Trust, a Norwegian public health trust. The work will focus on regions where HBV is endemic in Ethiopia and South Africa, and researchers will investigate patients’ responses to tenofovir, a first-line treatment for hepatitis B, which is also used to treat HIV. Prof Tongai Maponga, associate professor in the Division of Medical Virology and Head of the Viral Hepatitis Research Group at SU, described the Wellcome Discovery Award as a “highly prestigious and highly competitive grant”. “It will help us continue, and build on, the work we’ve been doing on viral hepatitis in South Africa, in Africa and globally, with the end result being that we will be able to assist our patients better,” he said. Maponga, who is also a senior medical scientist at the National Health Laboratory Service, said the work of his team at SU focuses largely on “understanding viral hepatitis in African settings and translating that evidence into improved prevention, diagnosis, treatment and policy”. “Our vision is a world where no person suffers from viral hepatitis, and our programme is centred on what works in real African health systems.” He described chronic hepatitis B as “a silent but terrible disease”, adding that an estimated 2-3 million people in South Africa live with HBV infection. “One of the consequences is that it causes liver disease, including liver cirrhosis, and may lead to primary liver cancer. This cancer affects people at a relatively young age, even as early as their 20s. When somebody is diagnosed with primary liver cancer, they barely survive for six months, and most die within a year because of late diagnosis. “We have various tools, including a vaccine which we give in South Africa, but this only started in 1996, meaning there are still many people who were not vaccinated and could be infected. So, there is still a huge number of people who need to be diagnosed and treated,” Maponga said. “When treating the disease, it’s important to ensure that the viral load is suppressed. Achieving viral suppression drastically reduces the risk of developing liver disease and primary liver cancer. “This research will answer the key question: Why are some patients unable to achieve viral suppression?” Besides the research into this question, the study will also draw on data from HEPSANET, an existing longitudinal registry of patients who are living with viral hepatitis in several African countries, including South Africa, in a bid to gather information on some of the factors that predict treatment outcomes. Maponga said he was delighted that the Wellcome award will bring together local colleagues from Tygerberg Hospital, Groote Schuur Hospital, the University of Cape Town and SU. “Building collaborations with fellow South African institutions are amazing. We tend to work in silos, so we don’t always speak with the same voice to draw attention to important matters,” he said. “With this grant, we can change this tendency.” Prof Philippa Matthews, Head of the HBV Elimination Laboratory at the Francis Crick Institute and leader of the B-ZERO research project, said the work will involve expanding and analysing HEPSANET’s huge repository of patient data. “There are gaps in our understanding of the diverse hepatitis B treatment outcomes, and whether different viral strains are more likely than others to develop resistance to drugs,” she said. The B-ZERO team will gather health and demographic information in clinical research sites, working to understand barriers to accessing and taking consistent therapy. “They’ll focus on assessing the impact of co-existing health conditions and the effect of suboptimal drug concentrations on treatment outcomes,” said Matthews. At the same time, another part of the team will be examining the biological aspects of the virus itself. “There is lots to be optimistic about if we scale up treatment,” Matthews said, “as we know it can reduce liver disease. “But,” she cautioned, “there is a risk of scaling up in a naïve way, without understanding the barriers in access, or tackling incomplete treatment responses.” Share FacebookXLinkedInEmailWhatsAppCopy Link Tags Health care Research Related stories Innovation and entrepreneurship Advancing innovation: New resource furthers AI-enabled health research at SU From improving public health communication to making cancer care more affordable and sifting through millions of genetic variants at speed, Stellenbosch... Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different
新闻简报本文于 2026 年 8 月 27 日发表在《美国管理护理杂志》上,讨论了乙型肝炎和丙型肝炎治疗方法之间的根本区别。它强调乙型肝炎的基因组整合使得真正的病毒学治愈比丙型肝炎的清除更加复杂。作者 Raymond Chung 医学博士和 Douglas Dieterich 医学博士解释说,一旦丙型肝炎被清除,病毒就不会整合到 基因组 中,而是仍局限于细胞质中,从而使其永久清除。相比之下,乙型肝炎整合到肝细胞 基因组 中,这意味着即使在表面抗原清除后它也可以持续存在。这种整合可能导致癌基因的持续刺激或抑癌基因的抑制,从而增加患肝癌的风险。文章强调,乙型肝炎的 功能性治愈 涉及失去表面抗原并减少临床终点,但它并不等于真正的病毒学治愈。它还指出,旨在从 基因组 中解离乙型肝炎 DNA 的疗法正在开发中,但尚未准备好用于临床。该文章是对当前研究和临床理解的信息回顾,没有报告具体的 暴发 数据或公共卫生行动。

时间

地点与对象
全球范围内,重点关注人类 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV) 感染及相关疾病状态。
事件
一篇文章讨论了乙型肝炎和丙型肝炎治疗之间的根本区别,强调乙型肝炎的基因组整合使得真正的病毒学治愈比丙型肝炎清除更加复杂。本文由医学博士 Raymond Chung 和医学博士 Douglas Dieterich 撰写。
规模、影响与风险
该文章强调了真正治愈乙型肝炎所面临的挑战,因为它融入了 宿主 基因组,这种药物可能会持续存在并可能重新激活。它不报告具体病例数、死亡数或暴露数量,但讨论了对 治疗 和管理的影响。

Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different

News Brief
This article, published on August 27, 2026, by the American Journal of Managed Care, discusses the fundamental differences between hepatitis B and hepatitis C cures. It highlights that hepatitis B's genomic integration makes a true virologic cure more complex than hepatitis C clearance. The authors, Raymond Chung, MD, and Douglas Dieterich, MD, explain that once hepatitis C is cleared, the virus does not integrate into the genome and remains confined to the cytoplasm, making its clearance permanent. In contrast, hepatitis B integrates into the hepatocyte genome, meaning it can persist even after surface antigen clearance. This integration can lead to ongoing stimulation of oncogenes or suppression of tumor-suppressor genes, increasing the risk of liver cancer. The article emphasizes that a functional cure for hepatitis B involves losing surface antigen and reducing clinical endpoints, but it does not equate to a true virologic cure. It also notes that therapies aimed at de-integrating hepatitis B DNA from the genome are in development but not yet ready for clinical use. The piece serves as an informative review of current research and clinical understanding, without reporting specific outbreak data or public health actions.

Play Mute Current Time 0:00 / Duration 0:00 Loaded: 0% Stream Type LIVE Seek to live, currently playing liveLIVE Remaining Time -0:00 1x Playback Rate Picture-in-PictureFullscreen Episodes in this series Previous slideNext slide EP. 1 Understanding the Immune Pathophysiology Driving Chronic Hepatitis B EP. 2 Hepatitis B Epidemiology: Closing the Screening and Diagnosis Gap EP. 3 Monitoring Disease Progression and Liver Cancer Risk in Hepatitis B EP. 4 Quantitative HBsAg Testing and the Path to Finite-Duration Therapy EP. 5 Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care Now Playing EP. 6 Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different This episode, "Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different," features the panel examining why hepatitis B's viral integration sets it apart from hepatitis C. Dr. Chung asks Dr. Dieterich to compare hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and to explain why the hepatitis B functional cure story differs fundamentally from the hepatitis C cure story that clinicians and payers already know. Dr. Dieterich explains that hepatitis C is a flavivirus, a family in which no other member, including dengue or yellow fever, ever becomes chronic. Once a patient is cured of hepatitis C, the virus does not integrate into the genome and stays confined to the cytoplasm, so clearance is truly permanent. He notes that liver cancer can still emerge in cured hepatitis C patients who had cirrhosis, but that risk stems from pre-existing cirrhotic damage, not any remaining virus. Hepatitis B behaves very differently, he says, describing it as closer to HIV, sometimes called a closet retrovirus because it cycles from DNA to RNA and back to DNA, integrating into the hepatocyte genome. That integration means the virus is never completely eliminated, even once surface antigen clears. He mentions that therapies aimed at de-integrating hepatitis B DNA from cccDNA and the hepatocyte genome exist but are not yet ready for clinical use. Because integrated DNA persists, it can continue stimulating oncogenes or suppressing tumor-suppressor genes even after antigen loss. Dr. Chung summarizes that functional cure means losing surface antigen and reducing clinical endpoints, but it does not represent a true virologic cure. He stresses that clinicians must remind patients and referring providers that the virus can still return through reactivation, since it never fully leaves the body the way hepatitis C does once cured. Our next episode, "The Next Frontier in Hepatitis B Functional and Virologic Cure," turns to the pipeline of therapies aiming to push cure rates even further. Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care - The American Journal of Managed Care

News Brief
The article titled 'Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care' published in The American Journal of Managed Care on 2026-08-27 discusses the challenges and considerations in managing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections, focusing on long-term antiviral safety and unmet clinical needs. It highlights the importance of addressing gaps in care and treatment, particularly in the context of chronic hepatitis B and its associated complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cirrhosis. The content includes insights from experts and references to related topics like hepatitis D and MASLD (Metabolic Associated Liver Disease). However, the article does not provide specific case counts, death tolls, or exposure numbers, nor does it detail any particular outbreak or event. Instead, it serves as a general review and analysis of current practices and future directions in hepatitis B management. The article is part of a broader discussion on population health and managed care strategies, emphasizing the need for improved access and tailored treatment approaches.

B 常规重要公共卫生新闻

乙型肝炎护理中未满足的需求和长期 抗病毒药物 安全性

Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care
新闻简报本文发表于 2026 年 8 月 27 日,讨论了管理 慢性乙型肝炎 方面持续存在的挑战,特别是在初级保健机构中。它强调了治疗指南中的不一致之处,例如AASLD使用的ALT和AST阈值与中国、EASL、APASL和WHO等其他指南不同。这些指南可治疗任何可检测到的病毒水平的乙型肝炎,而不需要升高肝酶。文章强调临床医生和初级保健医生之间需要更好的沟通,因为大多数乙型肝炎处方都是由他们开的。它还探讨了 功能性治愈 的概念及其对癌症风险和长期 抗病毒药物 安全性的影响。Dieterich 博士指出,即使 HBV DNA 水平无法检测到,由于整合的病毒 DNA,患肝细胞癌 (HCC) 的风险仍然存在。此外,文章还提到了持续 HCC 筛查的重要性以及血清转化后血清逆转的可能性,无论是自发的还是 治疗 诱导的。讨论强调了当前标准护理治疗与患者期望之间的差距,呼吁改进乙型肝炎管理策略。

时间
本集还探讨了 功能性治愈 对癌症风险和长期 抗病毒药物 安全性的意义。
地点与对象
美国,初级保健医生和 慢性乙型肝炎 患者。

B routine priorityPublic-health news

Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care

News Brief
This article, published on August 27, 2026, discusses the ongoing challenges in managing chronic hepatitis B, particularly in primary care settings. It highlights the inconsistency in treatment guidelines, such as the use of ALT and AST thresholds by AASLD, which differ from other guidelines like those from Chinese, EASL, APASL, and WHO. These guidelines treat hepatitis B at any detectable viral level without requiring elevated liver enzymes. The article emphasizes the need for better communication between clinicians and primary care physicians, as most prescriptions for hepatitis B are written by them. It also explores the concept of a functional cure and its implications for cancer risk and long-term antiviral safety. Dr. Dieterich notes that even with undetectable HBV DNA levels, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains due to integrated viral DNA. Additionally, the article mentions the importance of continued HCC screening and the potential for seroreversion after seroconversion, whether spontaneous or treatment-induced. The discussion underscores the gap between current standard-of-care therapy and patient expectations, calling for improved strategies in hepatitis B management.

Play Mute Current Time 0:00 / Duration 0:00 Loaded: 0% Stream Type LIVE Seek to live, currently playing liveLIVE Remaining Time -0:00 1x Playback Rate Picture-in-PictureFullscreen Episodes in this series Previous slideNext slide EP. 1 Understanding the Immune Pathophysiology Driving Chronic Hepatitis B EP. 2 Hepatitis B Epidemiology: Closing the Screening and Diagnosis Gap EP. 3 Monitoring Disease Progression and Liver Cancer Risk in Hepatitis B EP. 4 Quantitative HBsAg Testing and the Path to Finite-Duration Therapy Now Playing EP. 5 Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care EP. 6 Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different In "Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care," the panel explores where guideline adherence breaks down and what long-term antiviral safety data actually show. Dr. Chung asks why chronic hepatitis B still presents significant unmet needs in 2026 and how the gap between current standard-of-care therapy and patient and clinician expectations should be characterized. Dr. Dieterich notes that AASLD guidelines still include ALT and AST thresholds as treatment criteria, unlike Chinese, EASL, APASL, and World Health Organization guidelines, which do not require elevated liver enzymes and instead treat at essentially any detectable viral level. He adds that adherence to strict guidelines is inconsistent, particularly since the majority of U.S. hepatitis B prescriptions are written by primary care physicians. He sees a communication gap that needs to be closed with these prescribers. Turning to functional cure, Dr. Chung asks what improved cure rates mean for HCC risk, disease progression, and the possibility of permanently stopping therapy. Dr. Dieterich compares it to suppressing HBV DNA to undetectable levels, which dramatically lowers but does not eliminate HCC risk because integrated viral DNA remains. He says clearing surface antigen similarly lowers risk further without reaching zero, since patients retain core antibody and integrated DNA, so HCC screening must continue. He notes that seroreversion can occur even after seroconversion, whether spontaneous or treatment-induced, meaning clinicians can never fully trust the virus has left. Dr. Chung adds that patients need reminding of reactivation risk before chemotherapy, high-dose immunosuppression, or biologic therapy. The next episode in this series, "Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different," features the panel contrasting hepatitis B with hepatitis C's very different cure story. Hibsago (bepirovirsen) approved in Japan as first and only functional cure for chronic hepatitis B - GSK

News Brief
On August 24, 2026, GSK announced the approval of Hibsago (bepirovirsen) in Japan as the first and only functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. This marks a significant advancement in the treatment of the disease, which affects hundreds of millions of people globally. Chronic hepatitis B infections are known to increase the risk of liver cancer or cirrhosis, particularly if left untreated. The approval is based on GSK's research and development efforts in the therapeutic area of infectious diseases. No specific case or death counts were reported in the supplied evidence, but the implications of this development suggest a potential shift in the management of chronic hepatitis B. The source provides no indication of unresolved information or limitations in the approval process.

科威特研究测量注射吸毒者的乙型肝炎、丙型肝炎和艾滋病毒 - Bioengineer.org

Kuwait Study Measures Hepatitis B, C, HIV in People Who Inject Drugs - Bioengineer.org
新闻简报科威特国家成瘾治疗中心于2024年进行的一项研究发表在《BMC传染病》上,评估了注射吸毒者中乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)、丙型肝炎病毒(HCV)和人类免疫缺陷病毒(HIV)的患病率。结果显示,HBV 的 血清流行率 为 0.2%(1,255 名测试者中的 2 名),HCV 的抗 HCV 患病率 为 2.1%(1,169 名测试者中的 25 名),HIV 的 血清流行率 为 0.93%(1,287 名测试者中的 12 名)。乙型肝炎病毒和丙型肝炎病毒均通过分子检测得到证实,呈活动性病毒血症。该研究强调,乙肝病例数量较少限制了统计分析,而丙肝病毒结果表明存在显着的年龄相关性,在 50 岁或以上的参与者中,患病率 上升至 10.8%。HIV 结果显示,只有 66.7% 的血清阳性病例可检测到病毒血症,这可能是由于有效的抗逆转录病毒治疗所致。该研究强调需要改善该人群的 诊断 和 治疗 访问权限。
查看新闻五要素
时间
该研究在 2024 年进行,新闻报道于 2026 年 8 月 26 日发布。
地点与对象
该研究的重点是科威特国家戒毒中心 治疗 的注射毒品者,大多数参与者是男性和科威特国民。
事件
开展了一项横断面研究,以评估科威特注射吸毒者中 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV)、丙型肝炎病毒 (HCV) 和人类免疫缺陷病毒 (HIV) 的 患病率,研究结果发表在《BMC 传染病》上。
规模、影响与风险
HBV 的 血清流行率 为 0.2%(1,255 例检测中的 2 例),HCV 的抗 HCV 患病率 为 2.1%(1,169 例检测中的 25 例),HIV 的 血清流行率 为 0.93%(1,287 例检测中的 12 例)。该研究强调了积极的 传播 的潜力以及改善护理的需要。
应对、状态与不确定性
该研究使用血清学和分子检测来确认活动性感染。它指出,乙肝病例数量较少限制了统计分析,而丙肝病毒和艾滋病毒结果表明存在活动性病毒血症和 治疗 获取方面的差距。
B routine priorityPublic-health news

Kuwait Study Measures Hepatitis B, C, HIV in People Who Inject Drugs - Bioengineer.org

News Brief
A study conducted in Kuwait’s national addiction treatment center in 2024, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, assessed the prevalence of hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) among people who inject drugs. The findings revealed that HBV had a seroprevalence of 0.2% (2 out of 1,255 tested), HCV had an anti-HCV prevalence of 2.1% (25 out of 1,169 tested), and HIV had a seroprevalence of 0.93% (12 out of 1,287 tested). Both HBV and HCV were confirmed through molecular testing, showing active viremia. The study emphasized that the small number of HBV cases limited statistical analysis, while HCV results indicated a significant age-related correlation, with prevalence rising to 10.8% among participants aged 50 or older. HIV results showed that only 66.7% of seropositive cases had detectable viremia, possibly due to effective antiretroviral therapy. The research highlighted the need for improved diagnosis and treatment access in this population.

HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, August 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Kuwait Study Measures Hepatitis B, C, HIV in People Who Inject Drugs by Bioengineer August 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Kuwait’s national addiction treatment center is reporting a marked change in the blood-borne virus landscape among people who inject drugs, with hepatitis C virus (HCV) remaining closely linked to age and HIV appearing more prevalent than in a previous 2017 assessment. The findings come from a cross-sectional study of patients evaluated throughout 2024, offering one of the most recent national snapshots of hepatitis B virus (HBV), HCV, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection in this population. The study, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, examined both antibody or antigen evidence of infection and, where screening was positive, the presence of viral genetic material in blood. That distinction is critical: a positive serological test can indicate current infection, past exposure, or immune recognition, whereas nucleic acid testing identifies active viral replication and therefore a more immediate potential for transmission. The investigation enrolled 1,287 consecutive patients attending Kuwait’s national addiction treatment center between January and December 2024. Most participants were men, who represented 86.6% of the cohort, and 87.3% were Kuwaiti nationals. The median age was 33 years. Researchers screened blood samples using chemiluminescent immunoassays, laboratory techniques that detect specific immune markers or viral proteins through light-producing chemical reactions. For HBV, the principal screening marker was hepatitis B surface antigen, or HBsAg, a protein found on the surface of the virus and commonly used as an indicator of ongoing infection. HCV screening searched for antibodies generated in response to the virus, while HIV testing identified serological evidence of infection. Samples that reacted in screening were then subjected to nucleic acid testing to determine whether viral RNA or DNA could be detected. Discover more infection Ordering Infection Tests drug drugs The overall HBV result was low but clinically important. HBsAg was detected in two of 1,255 tested participants, corresponding to a seroprevalence of 0.2%. Both reactive samples were confirmed by molecular testing to contain active HBV viremia. HBV is a DNA virus that infects liver cells and can establish chronic infection, particularly when the immune system fails to clear the virus after exposure. Even a small number of active infections can matter in networks where needles, syringes, or other injection equipment are shared, because HBV is efficiently transmitted through infected blood and can persist outside the body longer than several other blood-borne viruses. The number of HBV-positive cases was too small to support reliable multivariable statistical analysis, so the researchers did not calculate adjusted risk estimates for this infection. HCV was detected in 25 of 1,169 participants, producing an overall anti-HCV prevalence of 2.1%. Unlike antibody screening alone, however, the molecular results showed that all 25 seropositive participants had detectable HCV RNA. In practical terms, every person identified through HCV serology in this cohort also had evidence of active infection at the time of testing. HCV is an RNA virus that can rapidly diversify within the body, helping it evade immune clearance and increasing the likelihood of chronic infection. Persistent HCV replication can cause progressive liver inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer, although modern direct-acting antiviral medicines can cure most infections after a relatively short course of treatment. The finding of universal detectable viremia therefore points not only to an infectious reservoir but also to a potentially treatable gap between diagnosis and care. Age emerged as the clearest statistical correlate of HCV infection. Prevalence increased significantly across age groups, with a reported probability value below 0.001, and reached 10.8% among participants aged 50 years or older. In the adjusted analysis, each increase in age was associated with higher odds of HCV infection, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.1 and a 95% confidence interval from 1.07 to 1.16. An odds ratio of this magnitude represents a gradual but meaningful accumulation of risk across the lifespan rather than a sudden change at one particular age. Older participants may have experienced more years of injection exposure, repeated contact with contaminated equipment, or earlier periods when harm-reduction services and antiviral treatment were less accessible. The cross-sectional design cannot establish which mechanism was responsible, but the age gradient is consistent with infection accumulating over time in a population exposed to recurrent blood contact. HIV was identified in 12 of the 1,287 participants, giving an overall seroprevalence of 0.93%. All HIV-positive cases were male, reflecting both the strong male predominance of the treatment-center cohort and a possible difference in exposure patterns that the study could not fully explain. Molecular testing detected HIV viremia in eight of the 12 seropositive participants, or 66.7%. A reactive HIV screening test therefore did not always correspond to detectable circulating virus in the available samples. This may reflect effective antiretroviral therapy, low-level infection below the assay’s detection threshold, or other clinical and laboratory factors; the abstract does not specify the treatment status of those participants. HIV is a retrovirus that converts its RNA genome into DNA and integrates that DNA into host cells, creating a lifelong infection that requires sustained antiretroviral therapy to suppress replication. In the multivariable model, female sex was associated with substantially lower odds of HIV infection than male sex, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.14, a 95% confidence interval of 0.02 to 0.92, and a reported p-value of 0.04. This estimate should be interpreted cautiously because the number of HIV-positive cases was very small and the cohort contained far more men than women. Small case counts can produce wide confidence intervals and make adjusted associations sensitive to the inclusion or exclusion of individual observations. Nevertheless, the result reinforces the need for prevention and testing strategies that account for the gendered structure of drug-use and treatment populations rather than assuming that a single intervention will reach all groups equally. The authors describe the HIV findings as a concerning increase compared with the center’s 2017 baseline, while also reporting a shift toward universal active HCV viremia among those with positive HCV serology. Direct comparison between years requires caution because changes in recruitment, testing methods, patient composition, treatment access, and the duration of injection exposure can all influence observed prevalence. Even so, the results reveal a critical weakness in the care cascade. Testing is only the first step: patients must receive confirmatory results, clinical evaluation, antiviral treatment when indicated, adherence support, and follow-up testing. For HCV, the fact that all 25 seropositive participants were viremic suggests that antibody detection was not identifying a large pool of people who had cleared infection or already been cured. Instead, it uncovered individuals who appeared to remain untreated or otherwise connected to active transmission networks. The study’s implications extend beyond the treatment center. The researchers call for expanded harm reduction, including reliable access to sterile injecting equipment, safer-injection education, vaccination and prevention services for HBV, and integrated screening for multiple blood-borne viruses. HCV test-and-treat programs could be particularly valuable because direct-acting antivirals can eliminate the virus, reduce the risk of liver disease, and lower the probability of onward transmission. HIV prevention must combine routine testing with rapid linkage to antiretroviral therapy, while people who test negative but remain at substantial risk may benefit from prevention counseling and, where clinically appropriate, pre-exposure prophylaxis. The molecular confirmation of active HBV and HCV infection also demonstrates why serological screening alone is insufficient for public health planning. Kuwait’s 2024 data depict a population in which infections remain concentrated but consequential, and where connecting diagnosis to treatment could transform viral surveillance into a measurable reduction in transmission and disease. Review Identifies Testable Framework for Hidden Genotype D Hepatitis B Mutation Clusters - Bioengineer.org

News Brief
A review published on August 27, 2026, by Bioengineer.org challenges the traditional understanding of occult hepatitis B infection, particularly in genotype D, which is prevalent in the Middle East. The study suggests that combinations of mutations in the virus’s surface protein may interact in ways that alter the antigen’s detectability, potentially explaining why some infected individuals test negative for HBsAg despite having replication-competent HBV DNA. This hypothesis, however, remains unproven and is based on a plausible framework rather than established mechanisms. The researchers highlight the need for more comprehensive datasets and statistical models to validate these interactions, as current evidence only reaches the first or second level of their proposed hierarchy. The implications of this research could affect diagnostic testing, blood-screening strategies, and vaccination programs, but no specific case counts or exposure numbers are provided in the evidence. The review underscores the importance of distinguishing between observation and speculation in understanding the complex genetic behavior of HBV.

HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, August 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Review Identifies Testable Framework for Hidden Genotype D Hepatitis B Mutation Clusters by Bioengineer August 27, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A Hidden Hepatitis B Problem May Depend on Combinations of Mutations, Not Just Single Genetic Changes A new review is challenging a widely used way of thinking about occult hepatitis B infection, a form of infection that can remain invisible to routine screening even while the virus persists in the body. The focus is hepatitis B virus genotype D, the dominant HBV lineage across much of the Middle East, where it provides the genetic background for diagnostic testing, blood-screening strategies and vaccination programmes. The review argues that individual mutations in the virus’s surface protein cannot fully explain why some infected people test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen, or HBsAg. Instead, combinations of mutations may interact in unexpected ways, altering the virus’s ability to produce, secrete or display the antigen. Such interactions, known as epistasis, could help explain how replication-competent HBV DNA survives in people whose standard blood tests appear negative. However, the researchers emphasise that this is a plausible hypothesis, not an established mechanism. Discover more Downloading Study Guides Tracking Market News Comparing College Programs Building Stock Portfolios Occult hepatitis B infection, or OBI, is defined by the presence of replication-competent HBV DNA in a person who tests negative for HBsAg, the viral marker most commonly used to identify active infection. Viral levels in OBI are often very low, which makes detection difficult and can allow cases to evade routine screening. The condition matters because apparently uninfected blood or organs may still carry transmissible virus, while immunosuppressive treatment can sometimes reactivate a quiet infection. HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus that replicates through an RNA intermediate, a process that permits genetic variation despite its DNA genome. Changes in the gene encoding the surface proteins can affect how antigens fold, assemble into particles or interact with antibodies. Some mutations are known to produce “immune escape” or “diagnostic escape,” enabling viral particles to avoid antibody recognition or reducing the amount of detectable HBsAg. Yet single substitutions explain only part of the clinical and laboratory variation observed in occult infection. The review centres on the possibility that mutations may work as a network rather than as isolated alterations. In genetics, epistasis occurs when the effect of one mutation depends on the presence of another. Two changes can reinforce each other, cancel each other out or generate a new phenotype that neither produces alone. For HBV, a mutation in one portion of the surface protein could alter the local structure in a way that changes the effect of a second mutation elsewhere. The combined result might influence the stability of the protein, its movement through the endoplasmic reticulum, its incorporation into viral or subviral particles, or its exposure to antibodies. A cluster might therefore reduce HBsAg secretion without eliminating viral replication. That distinction is crucial: a virus can remain biologically active while becoming harder to identify through an antigen-based assay. The authors propose that this type of non-additive interaction could be especially important in genotype D, but they find that direct evidence remains sparse. To separate observation from speculation, the researchers establish a four-level evidence hierarchy. The first level consists simply of mutations appearing together in sequence data, a pattern called co-occurrence. Co-occurrence can be suggestive, but it does not prove that the mutations interact biologically. The second level requires phylogenetically corrected covariation, which asks whether mutations continue to be associated after accounting for the fact that closely related viruses inherited the same changes from a common ancestor. Without this correction, researchers can mistake shared ancestry for functional cooperation. The third level requires an experiment comparing a candidate mutation cluster with each of its constituent single mutations on the same defined genotype D genetic background. The fourth and strongest level demands mechanistic validation, combining functional data with structural or biochemical evidence to explain how the mutations produce their effect. According to the review, existing studies reach only the first or second level. That evidence gap is significant because viral sequence databases can create an illusion of certainty. If several substitutions repeatedly appear in the same HBV genomes, they may seem to form a functional unit. But the pattern could instead reflect founder effects, regional transmission chains, sampling bias or the evolutionary history of a particular genotype. Genotype D-specific datasets large enough for reliable cluster-level analysis are limited, and Middle Eastern datasets are even more restricted. The problem is compounded by the fact that many studies sequence only a portion of the viral genome, examine small numbers of patients or lack detailed clinical information. A mutation observed in an HBsAg-negative patient may be relevant, but it may also be incidental or linked to another unmeasured change. The review therefore calls for larger, geographically diverse datasets, full-length or carefully targeted sequencing, and statistical models that correct for phylogeny, recombination and population structure before any mutation cluster is labelled epistatic. The authors also examine whether HIV or hepatitis C virus coinfection could shape the emergence of mutation combinations. Coinfections can alter immune pressure, treatment exposure and the cellular environment in which HBV replicates. In theory, these conditions might favour viral variants that would be rare during HBV infection alone. Patients receiving antiviral drugs may also experience selection pressures that change the composition of the viral population over time. However, the review finds no direct evidence linking HIV or HCV coinfection to the selection of particular HBV surface-protein mutation clusters associated with OBI. This absence does not rule out an effect; it indicates that the relevant studies have not yet been performed or have not included enough well-characterised patients. Demonstrating such a relationship would require longitudinal sampling, reliable coinfection histories, treatment data and deep sequencing capable of detecting low-frequency viral variants rather than only the dominant sequence in a blood sample. The decisive experiment proposed by the researchers is deliberately straightforward in principle, although technically demanding in practice. Scientists would reconstruct candidate mutation clusters by site-directed mutagenesis on a defined genotype D backbone, creating viral or expression constructs containing each individual mutation as well as the full combination. These matched constructs could then be tested for HBsAg production and secretion, intracellular retention, antibody binding and viral replication. Assays would need to distinguish between reduced antigen synthesis and impaired release of the surface protein. They would also need to measure whether a mutation cluster changes the ratio of viral particles to non-infectious subviral particles, which are abundant HBV surface-protein structures released from infected cells. A genuine epistatic effect would be demonstrated if the combined mutations produced a phenotype that could not be predicted from the single mutants, such as a disproportionately large loss of HBsAg detectability while replication remained measurable. Repeating the comparison across independent genotype D backbones would help establish that the result is not an artefact of one laboratory strain. Structural biology could reveal why a mutation cluster behaves differently from its individual components, but the review warns that current tools have limitations. Recent cryo-electron microscopy structures of HBsAg subviral particles have improved understanding of the surface-protein architecture, yet the flexible loops forming the so-called “a” determinant are not resolved at the detail required to interpret many cluster-level conformational changes. The a determinant is the principal immunological region recognised by antibodies generated through infection or vaccination. Small structural shifts there could affect assay binding without necessarily changing the virus’s capacity to replicate. But modelling such shifts from unresolved or low-resolution regions remains an inference, not a direct observation. The researchers suggest combining improved structural methods with biochemical measurements, antibody panels and computational modelling. A credible mechanism would need to connect the sequence changes to a measurable change in folding, oligomerisation, membrane insertion, secretion or antibody accessibility. The implications extend beyond a single viral genotype or one region of the world. If combinations of mutations contribute to diagnostic escape, routine assays designed around well-characterised individual variants may fail to recognise some infections, particularly when viral loads are low. That could complicate blood and organ safety, clinical decisions before immunosuppression and surveillance of chronic HBV transmission. It could also influence how laboratories interpret apparently discordant results, such as detectable HBV DNA alongside a negative HBsAg test. Still, the review does not claim that current screening systems are broadly ineffective, nor does it establish that epistatic clusters are enriched among Middle Eastern populations. Its central message is methodological: a mutation pattern should not be promoted to a causal explanation until it survives phylogenetic analysis and controlled functional testing. By defining the experiments needed to move from sequence association to biological proof, the authors turn an intriguing explanation for occult infection into a testable research programme. The outcome could sharpen diagnostic design while clarifying how HBV evolution operates beneath the threshold of conventional detection. GSK scores regulatory wins for chronic hepatitis B drug, cancer therapy - pharma.economictimes.indiatimes.com

News Brief
On August 24, 2026, GSK announced that its experimental drug bepirovirsen, branded as Hibsago, has been approved in Japan as the first and only functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. This approval is based on late-stage studies showing that the drug helped nearly one-in-five patients achieve a functional cure, offering a potential alternative to lifelong antiviral therapy. Additionally, the U.S. FDA granted priority review for dostarlimab (Jemperli) as a possible treatment for rectal cancer, with an action date set for February 2027. Jemperli, already approved for specific endometrial cancer subtypes, is not currently approved for rectal cancer anywhere in the world. The evidence does not report specific case counts, death counts, or risk levels associated with these developments. The regulatory actions are confirmed, with no unresolved information or source limitations noted.

Advt GSK said the approval was based on late-stage studies, which showed that the drug helped nearly one-in-five patients achieve a functional cure and raised hopes for a finite treatment course as an alternative to lifelong antiviral pills. Bepirovirsen is designed to tackle hepatitis B in three ways: by blocking viral DNA replication, lowering hepatitis B surface antigen levels in the blood, and boosting immune response for longer-lasting control of the disease. Brii Biosciences 距离乙型肝炎 功能性治愈 又近了一步,但未来仍不确定 - Drug Discovery News

Brii Biosciences inches closer to functional cure for hepatitis B but future is uncertain - Drug Discovery News
新闻简报Brii Biosciences has reported promising results from Phase 2b trials of their immunotherapy BRII-179 in combination with elebsiran and PEG-IFN alpha, suggesting a potential functional cure for hepatitis B. The trials showed HBsAg loss rates of 42.9% and 40% with different dosing strategies, indicating that the priming approach may be more effective. However, the future of Phase 3 trials remains uncertain due to ongoing arbitration with Vir Biotechnology, which could delay further development. Meanwhile, GSK's bepirovirsen has been approved in Japan and is under review in the US, Europe, Canada, and China. If approved, it could offer a six-month treatment option instead of lifelong antiviral therapy. The company emphasized that more long-term data is needed to confirm the effectiveness of their approach, and the results do not yet meet the true definition of a functional cure. The hepatitis B virus (HBV) affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, and current treatments only manage the infection without a cure.

Home/ Research Areas/ Infectious Disease & Vaccines News Brii Biosciences inches closer to functional cure for hepatitis B but future is uncertain New results from their Phase 2 trials show promise, but there could be issues moving to Phase 3. GSK's functional cure could be approved in the US before then. Written byAllison Whitten, PhD Aug 26, 2026| 3 min read Hepatitis B causes damage to the liver and affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide. Credit: iStock.com/SewcreamStudio Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 3:00 The hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine is up to 90 percent effective at preventing HBV when given within 24 hours after birth. But for the hundreds of millions of people around the world who have already acquired the viral infection that attacks their liver, there is no cure. Current standard treatments consist of daily, lifelong antiviral therapies where the virus still hides within liver tissue. Therapies that lead to a functional cure for HBV are in the works, with Brii Biosciences recently announcing results of their Phase 2b ENRICH and ENHANCE trials. The trials tested the immunotherapy, BRII-179 in combination with the siRNA drug elebsiran discovered by Alnylam Pharmaceuticals and licensed by Vir Biotechnology, and the FDA-approved antiviral PEG-IFN alpha (pegylated interferon-alpha). The new results suggest that a priming strategy whereby BRII-179 is introduced before treatment with elebsiran and PEG-IFN alpha could result in a new functional cure approach for patients. “These initial [end-of-treatment] data provide important insights into the relative performance of the ENRICH and ENHANCE study designs,” said David Margolis, Chief Medical Officer of Brii Biosciences, in the press release. An uncertain future While the company noted that they will share the full dataset at a scientific conference later this year, they noted in the recent report that the priming strategy studied in the ENRICH trial achieved hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss rates of 42.9 percent with five doses every three weeks and 40 percent with seven doses every two weeks. The addition of the siRNA drug elebsiran specifically produced higher functional cure rates compared to PEG-IFN alpha alone (which achieved a 10.2 percent functional cure rate). Continue reading below... Application NoteRevealing the assembly of HIV's integration complex Mass photometry helps researchers investigate the large and dynamic molecular assemblies that drive HIV integration and influence antiviral drug development. Read More The ENHANCE study, on the other hand, showed that concurrent administration of the three medications was not as effective, with a HBsAg loss rate of 25.5 percent. “While longer-term follow-up is needed to assess durability of the HBsAg loss, the data observed to date, together with EOT and post-EOT findings from multiple prior studies, are very consistent, suggesting that the ENRICH study design is preferred for a registrational study,” said Margolis in the statement. Despite the promising new priming approach with BRII-179, the company emphasized in the statement that future Phase 3 trials remain in limbo at this time due to ongoing arbitration with Vir Biotechnology. “In particular, the Company cannot invest in a Phase 3 clinical study of any elebsiran-containing combination therapy for HBV unless and until the claims in the Arbitration are satisfactorily resolved. The Company will continue to evaluate such developments and assess their impact on the continued viability of the elebsiran program, and update its shareholders and the public as and when appropriate in accordance with relevant requirements,” stated the company in the news release. The dispute centers around the manufacturing of elebsiran after Brii Biosciences filed a claim on April 16th, 2026 regarding a breach in their 2018 Collaboration, Option, and License Agreement and a letter agreement from 2024. Hope for another HPV functional cure around the corner With the future of Brii Biosciences’ combination treatment up in the air, patients with HBV have hope that another functional cure therapy may arrive sooner. On August 24th, GSK announced that Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare approved bepirovirsen, their antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) — representing the first time a functional cure for HBV has been approved. Though no direct head-to-head comparisons can be made between GSK and Brii Biosciences’ functional cure treatments at present because of major differences in study designs and patient populations — and end-of-treatment results do not yet meet the true definition of a functional cure — it’s possible that more long-term data could show an edge for Brii Biosciences. Their press release noted that based on a subgroup analysis from the ENRICH study, patients with higher baseline HBsAg levels (1,000-3,000 IU/mL) may still have beneficial immune responses, while GSK’s bepirovirsen achieved a lower functional cure rate in patients up to 3,000 IU/mL. The FDA accepted GSK’s New Drug Application for Priority Review, with a decision expected in late October. Reviews are also underway in Europe, Canada, and China. If approved, it could open up the first functional cure to patients all over the world and allow them a treatment option that can be completed in just six months instead of lifelong. View Full Profile Here are some related topics that may interest you: Infectious Disease & Vaccines, hepatitis B, immunotherapy, infectious disease, siRNA, vaccines Home/ Research Areas/ Infectious Disease & Vaccines News Scientists discover in vivo gene transfer behind extreme antibiotic resistance A new study showed environmental bacteria can transfer resistance genes to pathogens inside human lungs that were previously sensitive to antibiotics. The findings could prompt new treatments that block the gene transfer. Written byAllison Whitten, PhD Aug 5, 2026| 2 min read The study revealed that some pathogens are getting help from other bacteria to become resistant to antibiotics. Credit: iStock.com/Fahroni Download PDF Over the last several years, researchers in Pradeep Singh’s lab at the University of Washington observed something peculiar happening in the lungs of patients with cystic fibrosis. After giving them tobramycin — an inhaled antibiotic that achieves high concentrations in the lungs — the team noticed that the bacteria causing the lung infection suddenly became resistant. “We observed almost instantaneous 10,000 fold increases in tobramycin resistance,” Singh told DDN. That didn’t make sense, as antibiotic resistance generally develops gradually as the bacteria’s genome slowly acquires mutations. Singh’s team went digging for what could be causing such a rapid and drastic jump in resistance. By using long-read sequencing on hundreds of bacteria from patient samples, Sardar Karash, a postdoctoral researcher in Singh’s lab at the time, found the answer. The infection-causing bacteria in the lung were not becoming resistant on their own. Instead, environmental bacteria that made its way into the lungs transferred small circular DNA called plasmids into the genomes of the infecting pathogens. Gene transfer from the environmental bacteria “completely transformed the ability of lung pathogens to resist treatment,” said Singh. “We see environmental bacteria from time to time in patients' samples, but did not think they did much harm. I don't think that anymore.” Continue reading below... Application NoteRevealing the assembly of HIV's integration complex Mass photometry helps researchers investigate the large and dynamic molecular assemblies that drive HIV integration and influence antiviral drug development. Read More The researchers described the new mechanism recently in a paper published in Nature Microbiology. Uncovering the secrets of bacteria The researchers were surprised by the new findings, especially since the environmental bacteria they found were only seen once in the patient lung samples before disappearing. And, the environmental bacteria themselves are not generally able to infect humans. “Despite this, they were able to rapidly transfer resistance genes to infecting pathogens throughout the lungs,” said Singh. “We see environmental bacteria from time to time in patients' samples, but did not think they did much harm. I don't think that anymore.” —Pradeep Singh, University of Washington The newly discovered mechanism of in vivo gene transfer could mean that transiently-infecting environmental bacteria could help pathogens inside human organs in other ways, too. “If environmental bacteria can ferry resistance genes inside human organs, we have to worry about what other genes might be transferred,” Karash said in the press release. Beyond increasing resistance, it’s possible that these genes could make the infecting bacteria more adept at evading immune responses or acquiring nutrients. The new work adds to increasing evidence that infecting bacteria have many more strategies to ward off antibiotics than previously known. Researchers at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital recently published work showing that a subset of S. Pneumoniae cells are able to enter a transient low-activity state of antibiotic tolerance to survive treatment and then resume their growth afterwards. New strategies needed To fight back against the acquired boost in antibiotic resistance, drug developers may come up with new strategies to block in vivo gene transfer from environmental bacteria in the future. However, Singh noted that much more basic research into this novel topic is needed before that can happen. “We first need to understand what organisms can carry mobile genetic elements into infected human organs. Then we need to understand what types of mobile elements carry key resistance and virulence genes, and how they get taken up by resident pathogens,” he said. For now, the new discovery also emphasizes the importance of perseverance and creativity from scientists in basic research. “On a personal level, it was great to see how the lead researcher, Sardar Karash, dug into this problem. He just wouldn't let up. He pushed and pushed until he got the answer. That’s what it takes,” said Singh. View Full Profile Here are some related topics that may interest you: Infectious Disease & Vaccines, antibiotic resistance, bacteria, genes, lungs Home/ Research Areas/ Infectious Disease & Vaccines News The new drug compound that could treat measles outbreaks – and other viruses Researchers developed a highly tolerable oral antiviral against orthoparamyxoviruses like measles and human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 3. Written byAllison Whitten, PhD Jun 3, 2026| 3 min read The drug targets the virus’ polymerase, stopping it from replicating. Credit: iStock.com/quantic69 Download PDF The viruses that make up the orthoparamyxovirus subfamily — which includes the reemerging measles virus, the highly-lethal Nipah virus, and human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 3 (HPIV1 and HPIV3) that cause high mortality in vulnerable stem cell transplant patients — are extremely contagious and largely have no approved antiviral treatments. That could soon change. New research by Richard Plemper’s lab at Georgia State University led to the development of a new oral antiviral drug candidate that could broadly treat multiple orthoparamyxovirus viruses, including HPIV3 and measles. The work was published recently in Science Advances. Based on encouraging results in both rodents and non-rodent animal models, the advance could lead to a promising therapeutic option for the estimated three million annual cases of HPIV in the US that require treatment. Given that progression to pneumonia typically occurs over several days, an effective oral antiviral could also provide a clinically meaningful window to prevent serious complications. The new oral antiviral, known as GHP-88310, could also offer a much-needed option to treat measles in the midst of increasing endemic transmission in the US and throughout the world due to vaccine hesitancy. Plemper told DDN that the most exciting part of identifying the compound was seeing the “broad-spectrum activity across major pathogens of multiple orthoparamyxovirus genera, which is very unusual for a well-behaved non-nucleoside polymerase inhibitor such as GHP-88310 and demonstrates that this compound binds to a highly conserved druggable target site.” Continue reading below... Application NoteRevealing the assembly of HIV's integration complex Mass photometry helps researchers investigate the large and dynamic molecular assemblies that drive HIV integration and influence antiviral drug development. Read More Finding a better drug Before finding GHP-88310, the team identified a non-nucleoside inhibitor class of the paramyxovirus polymerase. However, the drug was not well tolerated in higher mammals like ferrets. Given the need for this medication to be used in pediatric and immunocompromised patients, the drug candidate must have high tolerability. To address the tolerability problem, the scientists developed GHP-88310, a chemical analog of the original screening hit. GHP-88310 was very well tolerated in ferrets and dogs even at daily doses in ferrets exceeding 2000mg/kg body weight. And, Plemper noted that it came as a surprise that GHP-88310 was not only much better tolerated but also even more efficacious against HPIV3 and measles in rodents and non-rodents than the original screening hit, as well as in human airway epithelium organoids — and suitable for once daily oral administration. The drug works by targeting the central cavity of the viral P-L polymerase complex, which prevents the virus from being able to replicate. Hope for measles outbreaks An oral therapeutic can be rapidly administered to outpatients, enjoys higher patience compliance than injectables, and is therefore suitable for outbreak control through pre- and postexposure prophylaxis of social contacts of an index case in addition to providing direct therapeutic benefit. —Richard Plemper, Georgia State University With measles outbreaks on the rise that have put the US in imminent danger of losing its measles elimination status, a novel antiviral treatment could not come soon enough. Typically, the strategy public health officials use to contain regional measles outbreaks is known as ring vaccination, in which direct and social contacts around an infected person are vaccinated. Yet, with increasing vaccine hesitancy in some population groups, ring vaccination is no longer a viable option in some communities. A drug like GHP-88310 could therefore be the next best thing. “An oral therapeutic can be rapidly administered to outpatients, enjoys higher patience compliance than injectables, and is therefore suitable for outbreak control through pre- and postexposure prophylaxis of social contacts of an index case in addition to providing direct therapeutic benefit,” said Plemper. His team now has plans to advance the drug into formal preclinical development and prepare an Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling safety package, moving closer to their goal of finally getting a broad antiviral option for a variety of orthoparamyxoviruses. 日本批准 GSK 的 Hibsago 作为 慢性乙型肝炎 的首个 功能性治愈 - AllSci

Japan approves GSK's Hibsago as first functional cure for chronic hepatitis B - AllSci
新闻简报日本厚生劳动省 (MHLW) 已批准葛兰素史克 (GSK) 的 Hibsago (bepirovirsen) 成为首个治疗成人 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 的 功能性治愈。该批准基于在 29 个国家进行的 III 期试验的汇总数据,涉及 NA 治疗的成人,基线 HBsAg 水平为 3,000 IU/ml 或以下,HBV DNA 低于 90 IU/ml。结果显示,贝匹罗韦森组(1,220 名参与者中的 233 名)的 功能性治愈 率为 19%,而安慰剂组的 功能性治愈 率为 0%,其中一个亚组的 功能性治愈 率为 26%。该药物采用为期六个月的皮下注射疗程,并根据日本的 SENKU 指定进行审查,用于解决高度未满足的医疗需求的创新药物。GSK 报告称,49% 的贝匹罗韦森接受者在第 72 周时将 HBsAg 降低至 100 IU/ml 或更低,这是与增强免疫控制相关的阈值。该批准先于其他市场的监管决定,包括美国 FDA 和中国,贝匹罗韦森已在这些市场获得快速指定。
查看新闻五要素
时间
日本厚生劳动省 (MHLW) 于 2026 年 8 月 25 日批准了 Hibsago。该批准基于在 29 个国家进行的 III 期试验的汇总数据,结果显示总体人群中的 功能性治愈 率为 19%,基线 HBsAg 为 1,000 IU/ml 或以下的亚组中的 功能性治愈 率为 26%。
地点与对象
日本,专门针对患有 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 的成年人,他们之前接受过至少六个月的核苷(酸)类似物 (NA) 治疗并符合预先定义的病毒标志物。
事件
日本批准 GSK 的 Hibsago(贝匹罗韦森)作为成人 慢性乙型肝炎 的首个 功能性治愈,基于临床试验数据显示与安慰剂相比,功能性治愈 率显着。
规模、影响与风险
该批准涵盖基线 HBsAg 水平为 3,000 IU/ml 或以下且 HBV DNA 低于 90 IU/ml 的成年患者。汇总结果显示,贝匹罗韦森(1,220 名参与者中的 233 名参与者)的 功能性治愈 率为 19%,而安慰剂组的 功能性治愈 率为 0%。此外,49% 的贝匹罗韦森接受者在第 72 周时将 HBsAg 降低至 100 IU/ml 或更低,这表明免疫控制有改善的潜力。
应对、状态与不确定性
日本的 SENKU 指定加速了审批速度,该指定授予解决高度未满足的医疗需求的创新药物。厚生劳动省的审查基于 III 期试验数据,这是贝匹罗韦森的全球首次批准。该药物以六个月的皮下注射疗程给药。

Japan approves GSK's Hibsago as first functional cure for chronic hepatitis B - AllSci

News Brief
Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) has approved GSK's Hibsago (bepirovirsen) as the first functional cure for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in adults. The approval is based on pooled data from Phase III trials conducted across 29 countries, involving NA-treated adults with baseline HBsAg levels of 3,000 IU/ml or below and HBV DNA below 90 IU/ml. The results showed a 19% functional cure rate with bepirovirsen (233 of 1,220 participants) versus 0% with placebo, with a subgroup achieving 26% functional cure. The drug is administered as a six-month subcutaneous injection course and was reviewed under Japan's SENKU designation for innovative medicines addressing high unmet medical need. GSK reported that 49% of bepirovirsen recipients achieved HBsAg reduction to 100 IU/ml or below by week 72, a threshold linked to enhanced immune control. This approval precedes regulatory decisions in other markets, including the US FDA and China, where bepirovirsen has received expedited designations.

NewsPricingLoginSign up News·Regulatory & Policy Regulatory & Policy Japan approves GSK's Hibsago as first functional cure for chronic hepatitis B Edited by Robert McTiernan·August 25, 2026·2 min read Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in adults who have received at least six months of prior nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy and meet pre-defined viral markers — marking the first global approval for the antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and the first approval for a CHB therapy capable of achieving functional cure in patients. GSK licensed bepirovirsen from Ionis Pharmaceuticals and led its development. The approval covers adult patients with baseline hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/ml or below and hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA below 90 IU/ml at treatment initiation. Bepirovirsen is administered as a six-month subcutaneous injection course. The MHLW review was accelerated under Japan's SENKU designation, which is granted to innovative medicines addressing high unmet medical need. As an ASO, bepirovirsen targets HBV RNA to suppress production of viral proteins including HBsAg, with the goal of enabling immune-mediated control without ongoing antiviral therapy. Approval was supported by pooled data from the Phase III B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 trials, global randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies conducted across 29 countries in NA-treated adults with baseline HBsAg of 3,000 IU/ml or below. The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants achieving functional cure — defined as undetectable HBsAg and HBV DNA below the lower limit of quantification for at least 24 weeks after stopping all treatment. Pooled results showed a 19% functional cure rate with bepirovirsen (233 of 1,220 participants) versus 0% with placebo (p<0.001 in both trials); in the subgroup with baseline HBsAg of 1,000 IU/ml or below, the rate reached 26% (200 of 768). Current NA therapy typically achieves less than 1% functional cure, as noted by GSK. The AllSci BriefSystematic R&D and deal news. Daily. Subscribe GSK reported that 49% of bepirovirsen recipients in the overall population achieved HBsAg reduction to 100 IU/ml or below by week 72, a threshold associated in the medical literature with enhanced immune control and improved outcomes. The Japan approval precedes regulatory decisions in other markets where bepirovirsen has received expedited designations, including US FDA Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review status, with a PDUFA date expected in Q4 2026, and Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review designation in China, where GSK has partnered with Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical for commercialization. In the competitive CHB functional cure landscape, several companies are developing small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapies designed to drive HBsAg loss, including Arbutus Biopharma's imdusiran. GSK Wins Approval for New Hepatitis B Drug - EMJ
新闻简报葛兰素史克 (GSK) 的 慢性乙型肝炎 药物贝匹罗韦森 (bepirovirsen) 在日本获得全球首个批准,品牌为 Hibsago。此次批准标志着该国第一个也是唯一一个针对 慢性乙型肝炎 的 功能性治愈,据世界卫生组织称,该国估计有超过 800,000 人患有这种疾病。该药物在成功的后期试验后获得批准,该试验证明其能够帮助五分之一的患者实现 功能性治愈。Bepirovirsen 的作用是阻断病毒 DNA 复制,降低血液中乙型肝炎表面抗原水平,并增强 免疫应答 来长期控制病毒。该公司还宣布,FDA 将优先审查 Jemperli 作为治疗局部晚期直肠癌的潜在 治疗,行动日期定为 2027 年 2 月。这些监管胜利是葛兰素史克扩大肿瘤学和其他治疗领域药物开发管道的更广泛战略的一部分。此次批准是慢性乙型肝炎的治疗的一个重要里程碑,为终身抗病毒药物治疗提供了替代方案。
