There is a lot of misunderstanding surrounding vaccines, but their greatest value is in creating the antibodies to fight off initial infections, writes Walter Tsou.Read moreLM Otero / AP by Walter Tsou, For The Inquirer Published Aug. 27, 2026, 10:01 a.m. ET Listen to article • 0:00 min Imagine you are a general about to go to war. The enemies are known to be fierce fighters. Would you rather have three soldiers on your side or 300,000? Let’s personalize it. You are the general of your body under attack by a new flesh-eating bacterium. Would you rather have three antibodies on your side or 300,000 antibodies? Survival or death? Pretty easy choice. There is a lot of misunderstanding surrounding vaccines, but their greatest value is in creating the antibodies to fight off initial infections. President Donald Trump, now playing a role as pseudo-physician, has announced an executive order to reduce the number of childhood vaccines from 17 to 11. Hepatitis B, one of the nastiest viruses, is among the vaccines that are no longer required. Hepatitis B is a highly infectious virus, even more infectious than HIV. Undetected, it can pass from a mother who is carrying the virus to a baby during birth, infecting the newborn on Day One of life. Months later, the virus has infected the liver, causing the newborn to be fatigued, not eating, maybe even jaundiced. Years later, they can develop chronic hepatitis B and even liver failure or cancer. What is remarkable is that all of this is preventable with a vaccine administered at birth. Americans are very concerned about healthcare costs. The greatest way to cut healthcare costs is to prevent the disease in the first place. The more antibodies in our bodies able to fight the onslaught of viruses out in this hostile world, the more likely we will be in preventing disease in the first place. People, including Trump, wonder why there are so many vaccines. There are three factors: First is that there are a lot of bacterial and viral diseases. Each needs its own unique antibodies to fight them. There are a lot more than just 11 or even 17 viruses or bacteria in the world — which is why new recommendations and combinations are tested and recommended. Second is that researchers can measure antibody levels, and building up enough antibodies to defeat diseases may require more than one shot. At least two current vaccines can prevent cancer. Finally, viruses are very tricky and can mutate, camouflaging their detection from existing antibodies. Classic viruses that have this capability are influenza and SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19). So recommendations have changed to reflect the changing flu and COVID shots to be given annually rather than just once and done. Vaccine researchers are on the cusp of even greater breakthroughs. At least two current vaccines can prevent cancer. The HPV vaccine prevents human papillomavirus from infecting the cervix, which, in turn, prevents cervical cancer. HPV has also been linked to head and neck cancer. And the aforementioned hepatitis B vaccine can help prevent liver cancer. The Nobel Prize-winning discovery of mRNA vaccines developed by Philadelphia scientists is being used to create inactive tumor proteins that our immune system can recognize. Future researchers will be able to identify our personal cancers, create individual tumor proteins that our immune systems will recognize, and create a personalized immune response that can kill cancers in our bodies. These are heady times in medical research, which desperately needs the support of our government. Unfortunately, many of these discoveries, including new vaccines against scourges like Ebola, bird flu, hantavirus, malaria, and many others, are being stopped by our failure to invest in research. It is a lost opportunity to prevent disease using our own bodies’ immune system by creating an army of antibodies at the ready. And nothing is more frightening than trying to fight a virus with only three antibodies. Walter Tsou is the former health commissioner of Philadelphia and the past president of the Philadelphia County Medical Society. Scale, impact and risk
The article states that hepatitis B is a highly infectious virus, even more infectious than HIV, and can lead to chronic infection, liver failure, and cancer. It emphasizes that these outcomes are preventable with a vaccine administered at birth (N16, N17, N18, N19, N20).

GSK的Hibsago获日本批准,成为首款慢性乙型肝炎功能性治愈药物 - 富途牛牛

News article (Chinese original; verified English title unavailable)
新闻简报2026 年 8 月 25 日,MT Newswires 报道称,葛兰素史克的研究疗法 Hibsago 已获得日本卫生当局的批准,这标志着该药物首次被指定为 慢性乙型肝炎 的 功能性治愈。此次批准针对的是日本慢性乙型肝炎病毒感染者,标志着 治疗 范式的潜在转变,旨在实现持续病毒抑制,无需终身治疗。该公告不包括患者数量、临床结果或安全概况的数据,也没有提供有关批准后监测或分配计划的其他信息。因此,虽然监管决定代表了一个重要的里程碑,但更广泛的公共卫生影响和任何相关风险仍有待澄清。
查看新闻五要素
时间
MT Newswires 于 2026 年 8 月 25 日(08/25 01:51)报道了该批准。
地点与对象
日本;该批准适用于 慢性乙型肝炎 感染患者。
事件
据 MT Newswires 报道,GSK 的药物 Hibsago 在日本获得监管批准,成为第一个被归类为 慢性乙型肝炎 的药物。
规模、影响与风险
所提供的证据中未报告。
应对、状态与不确定性
监管部门的批准表明了官方回应,但报告中未提供有关推出、上市后 监测 或风险评估的更多详细信息。
B routine priorityPublic-health news

News article (Chinese original; verified English title unavailable)

Original title (Chinese)
GSK的Hibsago获日本批准,成为首款慢性乙型肝炎功能性治愈药物 - 富途牛牛
News Brief
On August 25, 2026, MT Newswires reported that GSK's investigational therapy Hibsago has been granted approval by Japanese health authorities, marking the first instance of a drug being designated a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. The approval targets individuals living with chronic HBV infection in Japan and signals a potential shift in treatment paradigms, aiming for sustained viral suppression without lifelong therapy. The announcement did not include data on patient numbers, clinical outcomes, or safety profiles, and no additional information on post‐approval monitoring or distribution plans was provided. As a result, while the regulatory decision represents a significant milestone, the broader public‐health impact and any associated risks remain to be clarified.

News Brief
On August 24, 2026, GSK received global approval for Hibsago, the first drug targeting chronic hepatitis B. This news was reported by Moomoo, a financial information and trading platform. The approval marks a significant development in the treatment of chronic hepatitis B, but the supplied evidence does not include specific case counts, death counts, or health-system impacts. The report is a financial news item and does not provide details on the drug's efficacy or public health response. The information is not subject to review by any regulatory body, and the content is intended for informational and educational purposes only, not as investment advice.
